demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Going to or near the place where the event happened
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed
I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: For a trauma defined as accidentally causing serious injury to another, 'Avoid Perpetrator Cues' is hard to reconcile because it implies the patient was harmed by a perpetrator rather than being the agent who injured someone else. That is a direct mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Humiliation' is not impossible after this trauma, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear link to the accidental-injury context; the dominant themes would more plausibly be guilt, responsibility, or fear of causing harm again. It is weaker than the perpetrator-cue problem but still clinically questionable here.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another, unless there was also significant injury or disfigurement to the patient; no other selected items indicate patient bodily injury, making this appraisal clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used as distraction is not impossible, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other items emphasize guilt, threat vigilance, and cue-triggered distress related to the accident, whereas self-harm implies a severe affect-regulation strategy not supported elsewhere in the selected items. This strategy is therefore clinically poorly anchored in the presented formulation/profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, a burnt smell implies a fire/burning context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no matching memory content or appraisal theme tied to smoke/fire, this trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People are not what they seem' suggests interpersonal mistrust/paranoia, which is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile centered on guilt and failure to protect after accidentally injuring another person. It does not connect plausibly to the listed triggers or strategies and is not supported by any interpersonal threat content.

vignette: Luca had always been a dancer at heart. For decades, he had twirled across stages, entertaining crowds with his energetic performances. But one fateful evening, while rushing to a show, Luca's car struck a pedestrian, leaving the young woman with severe injuries. The accident shook him to his core, and the once-carefree dancer began to unravel. As time passed, certain triggers started to haunt Luca. Whenever he heard songs that had been playing on the radio during the drive, he felt an overwhelming sense of dread wash over him. The catchy tunes now served as a cruel reminder of that terrible night, transporting him back to the scene of the accident. Similarly, crowded spaces began to unnerve him; the thought of being surrounded by people made his mind wander to the chaos and panic that followed the crash. Luca couldn't shake off the memory of the accident, replaying it in his head like a gruesome loop. He dwelled on how he used to be before the event - carefree, confident, and full of life. He missed those days, but they seemed irretrievable now. To cope with these painful memories, Luca started avoiding places that reminded him of the accident, steering clear of streets where it had happened. He even suppressed thoughts about the trauma, pushing them deep into his mind in a desperate attempt to silence the guilt and self-blame. However, these maladaptive strategies only seemed to fuel his distress. The weight of his perceived failure as a protector - he should have done more to prevent the accident - continued to haunt him. He couldn't forgive himself for not being able to save the young woman from harm, and this inaction guilt gnawed at his conscience day and night. Luca felt like he had failed in his most important role in life: as a guardian of others' safety. As these negative appraisals took hold, they began to shape his perception of the world around him. He started to notice cars hitting each other by accident - or even just slowing down at intersections - and would immediately think of that fateful night. These flashbacks left Luca on edge, always ready for disaster to strike again. His concentration waned, making it difficult to focus on anything else. Even when he knew he was in a safe place, his body remained tense, as if anticipating the next catastrophe. The resulting hypervigilance began to disrupt his life, especially at night. Luca found himself lying awake for hours, too alert to relax and fall asleep. His exhaustion only exacerbated the anxiety that had taken up residence within him. Certain triggers - those songs, crowded spaces - now seemed even more menacing than before, feeding into the cycle of fear and self-doubt. In his line of work as a dancer, these symptoms were becoming increasingly debilitating. Luca's usual performances were marred by mistakes and missed cues, as if his brain was stuck in an endless loop of threat monitoring. The lack of control over his thoughts and emotions terrified him - what would happen to his career? To his relationships? It was only when his wife expressed her concern about the strain on their relationship that Luca realized he needed help. He couldn't bear the thought of losing everything he held dear due to this all-consuming anxiety. As he sat in the therapist's office, he hoped for one thing: to find a way out of this suffocating cycle and rediscover his passion for life - or at least learn to forgive himself enough to live with it.
